results.title: WhatsApp marketing broadcast
results.answer:
I'll build this, but one thing has to change first: **"every phone number in our customer database" can't be the audience.** A WhatsApp promo is direct marketing by electronic communication, so **s69** applies. You may only send it to people who either:

1. **Opted in** (s69(1)(a)): a recorded, unticked opt-in on Form 4 or something substantially similar, covering WhatsApp and the kind of products you're promoting; or
2. **Fit the existing-customer exception** (s69(3)). All of these must hold:
   - you got their number **in the context of a sale** of a product or service (a real purchase, not just a sign-up or enquiry);
   - the promo is for **your own similar** products or services;
   - they were given a free, simple chance to **opt out when you collected the number**, and you offer it again in **every** message;
   - they have **not opted out**.

Anyone else in the table (leads, enquiries, imported or bought lists, people who said STOP) is excluded. Opt-out on its own doesn't count as consent (amended Regulations, 2025). The Regulator's first direct-marketing fine (FT Rams Consulting, R100 000) was for ignoring opt-outs, so this flow treats STOP as a hard stop.

There is also a **separate platform rule**: Meta's WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy requires an opt-in to receive WhatsApp messages from you. Meeting POPIA's existing-customer exception doesn't satisfy Meta's rule, so the query below needs both.

So this is two n8n workflows: the **Friday broadcast**, which only sends to eligible people, and an **opt-out handler** that catches STOP replies. I've assumed Postgres or Supabase and the WhatsApp Business Cloud API. Tell me if you use something else.

---

## 1. Database: the eligibility rules live in SQL, not in n8n

Keeping the rules in the database means anyone who reads the schema can see them, and n8n can't get round them.

```sql
-- ============================================================
-- POPIA inventory (s13 purpose, s14 retention, s17 documentation)
-- Store: privacy.consent_events / privacy.marketing_suppression / privacy.marketing_sends
-- Purpose: weekly WhatsApp promotions for our own products
-- Lawful basis: s69(1) opt-in consent OR s69(3) existing-customer exception
-- Special PI: no | Children: no (exclude under-18s)
-- Operators: n8n (host), Meta (WhatsApp Cloud API) -> s72 transfer, record ground
-- Retention: consent + suppression = life of relationship + 3 yrs (proof, s11(2)(a));
--            send log = 12 months
-- ============================================================

create schema if not exists privacy;

-- Append-only consent evidence (never UPDATE; withdrawal is a new row)
create table if not exists privacy.consent_events (
  id             uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  subject_id     uuid not null references public.customers(id),
  purpose        text not null,          -- 'marketing_whatsapp', 'whatsapp_platform_optin'
  action         text not null check (action in ('granted','withdrawn','optout_offered')),
  notice_version text not null,          -- version/hash of the exact wording shown
  wording        text not null,
  channel        text not null,          -- 'checkout','web_form','whatsapp_reply','in_store'
  source_url     text,
  created_at     timestamptz not null default now()
);

create or replace view privacy.consent_current as
select distinct on (subject_id, purpose) subject_id, purpose, action, created_at
from privacy.consent_events
where action in ('granted','withdrawn')
order by subject_id, purpose, created_at desc;

-- Global suppression: an opt-out from ANY channel blocks WhatsApp promos (DM-07)
create table if not exists privacy.marketing_suppression (
  phone_e164  text primary key,
  reason      text not null,             -- 'whatsapp_stop','email_unsub','complaint','meta_block'
  created_at  timestamptz not null default now()
);

-- Send log: IDs only, no phone numbers or message bodies (keeps PI out of logs)
create table if not exists privacy.marketing_sends (
  id            bigserial primary key,
  customer_id   uuid not null,
  campaign      text not null,           -- e.g. '2026-10-23-friday-promo'
  template_name text not null,
  basis         text not null,           -- 's69_1_consent' | 's69_3_existing_customer'
  wa_message_id text,
  status        text not null,           -- 'sent' | 'failed'
  sent_at       timestamptz not null default now()
);

alter table privacy.consent_events        enable row level security;
alter table privacy.marketing_suppression enable row level security;
alter table privacy.marketing_sends       enable row level security;
-- No client policies: only the n8n DB role or service role on the server reads or writes these.

-- ============================================================
-- The audience. n8n may ONLY read from this view.
-- ============================================================
create or replace view privacy.whatsapp_promo_audience as
select c.id as customer_id,
       c.first_name,
       c.phone_e164,
       case when mk.action = 'granted' then 's69_1_consent'
            else 's69_3_existing_customer' end as basis
from public.customers c
left join privacy.consent_current mk
       on mk.subject_id = c.id and mk.purpose = 'marketing_whatsapp'
left join privacy.consent_current wa
       on wa.subject_id = c.id and wa.purpose = 'whatsapp_platform_optin'
where c.phone_e164 ~ '^\+27[0-9]{9}$'                          -- normalised SA mobile
  and coalesce(c.is_minor, false) = false                       -- s34/s35: no promos to children
  and coalesce(mk.action, 'none') <> 'withdrawn'                -- opted out = never
  and not exists (select 1 from privacy.marketing_suppression s
                  where s.phone_e164 = c.phone_e164)            -- cross-channel opt-outs
  and (mk.action = 'granted' or wa.action = 'granted')          -- Meta opt-in to WhatsApp
  and (
        mk.action = 'granted'                                   -- route 1: s69(1) opt-in
     or (                                                       -- route 2: s69(3)
          exists (select 1 from public.orders o
                  where o.customer_id = c.id and o.status = 'paid')   -- (a) obtained in a sale
          and exists (select 1 from privacy.consent_events e
                      where e.subject_id = c.id
                        and e.purpose = 'marketing_whatsapp'
                        and e.action = 'optout_offered')                -- (c) opt-out offered at collection
        )
      );

-- Least-privilege DB user for n8n
create role n8n_marketing login password '<from secret manager>';
grant usage on schema privacy to n8n_marketing;
grant select on privacy.whatsapp_promo_audience to n8n_marketing;
grant insert on privacy.marketing_sends, privacy.marketing_suppression,
                privacy.consent_events to n8n_marketing;
grant usage on sequence privacy.marketing_sends_id_seq to n8n_marketing;
```

> If you have **no record** of whether existing customers were offered an opt-out when you collected their numbers, route 2 returns nobody. That's deliberate. The burden of proof is on you (s11(2)(a)), and you can't backfill that evidence. Fix it at checkout from now on (wording below), and ask existing customers for opt-in consent once (s69(2)).

---

## 2. Workflow A: Friday promo broadcast

**Workflow settings:** Timezone `Africa/Johannesburg`. Save successful executions: **off**. Save failed executions: **on**, pruned (see section 4).

| # | Node | Config |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Schedule Trigger** | Cron `0 10 * * 5` (Fridays 10:00 SAST, within CPA-permitted marketing hours) |
| 2 | **Code: skip public holidays** | Returns `[]` on SA public holidays, e.g. Good Friday (list below) |
| 3 | **Postgres: Get audience** | Credential = `n8n_marketing` role. Query below |
| 4 | **Loop Over Items** (Split in Batches) | Batch size 50 |
| 5 | **WhatsApp Business Cloud: Send Template** | Approved *Marketing* template, see section 5 |
| 6 | **Wait** | 1 second between batches (throughput and quality rating) |
| 7 | **Postgres: Log send** | Insert into `privacy.marketing_sends` (IDs only) |
| 8 | **IF: error = user blocked/opted out** | If true, insert into `marketing_suppression` |

**Node 2: skip public holidays (Code node)**
```js
// Keep this list current every year (Public Holidays Act + any declared days)
const holidays = ['2026-12-25', '2027-03-26' /* Good Friday 2027 */, '2027-04-27'];
const today = new Date().toLocaleDateString('en-CA', { timeZone: 'Africa/Johannesburg' });
return holidays.includes(today) ? [] : [{ json: { run: true, campaign: `${today}-friday-promo` } }];
```

**Node 3: audience query.** Fetch only what the message needs (s10 minimality).
```sql
select customer_id, first_name, phone_e164, basis
from privacy.whatsapp_promo_audience;
```
This runs **at send time**, not when a list was built, so someone who replied STOP on Thursday is excluded on Friday.

**Node 5: Send Template**
- Phone number ID: your WhatsApp Business number
- Recipient: `{{ $json.phone_e164 }}`
- Template: `friday_promo_v3` (language `en`)
- Body parameter 1: `{{ $json.first_name }}`
- Settings: **On Error → Continue (using error output)**, so one failure doesn't stop the run, and node 8 handles it.

**Node 7: log send**
```sql
insert into privacy.marketing_sends (customer_id, campaign, template_name, basis, wa_message_id, status)
values ($1, $2, 'friday_promo_v3', $3, $4, $5);
-- $1 = {{ $('Loop Over Items').item.json.customer_id }}
-- $2 = {{ $('Code: skip public holidays').first().json.campaign }}
-- $3 = {{ $('Loop Over Items').item.json.basis }}
-- $4 = {{ $json.messages?.[0]?.id ?? null }}
-- $5 = {{ $json.messages ? 'sent' : 'failed' }}
```

**Node 8:** if Meta's error says the recipient has chosen to stop marketing messages from your business, insert the number into `privacy.marketing_suppression` with reason `meta_block`.

---

## 3. Workflow B: STOP and opt-out handler (build this before the first send)

| # | Node | Config |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **WhatsApp Trigger** | Updates: `messages`. If you use a plain Webhook node instead, verify Meta's `X-Hub-Signature-256` HMAC with your app secret and reject anything unsigned |
| 2 | **Code: detect opt-out** | Below |
| 3 | **IF** `optOut === true` | |
| 4 | **Postgres: record withdrawal** | Below |
| 5 | **WhatsApp: send text** | Confirmation (service reply, no promo content) |
| 6 | *(optional)* **HTTP Request** | Push the suppression to your email/SMS tool so the opt-out applies on every channel |

**Node 2**
```js
const msg = $json.messages?.[0];
if (!msg) return [];
const text = (msg.text?.body || msg.button?.text || msg.interactive?.button_reply?.title || '')
  .trim().toLowerCase();
const STOP = ['stop', 'stop promotions', 'unsubscribe', 'opt out', 'optout', 'cancel', 'remove me'];
return [{ json: {
  phone_e164: '+' + msg.from,          // Cloud API sends 27821234567
  optOut: STOP.some(w => text === w || text.startsWith(w)),
}}];
```

**Node 4**
```sql
insert into privacy.marketing_suppression (phone_e164, reason)
values ($1, 'whatsapp_stop')
on conflict (phone_e164) do nothing;

insert into privacy.consent_events (subject_id, purpose, action, notice_version, wording, channel)
select id, 'marketing_whatsapp', 'withdrawn', 'n/a', 'Replied STOP on WhatsApp', 'whatsapp_reply'
from public.customers where phone_e164 = $1;
```

**Node 5 text:** "Done. You won't get promotional WhatsApps from [Trading name] any more. Order updates will still come through. Questions? privacy@yourdomain.co.za"

Treat free-text complaints such as "how did you get my number?" as objections too (s11(3)). Route them to a person rather than relying on keyword matching.

---

## 4. n8n hardening (it's an operator holding customer PI)

Self-hosted (`.env`):
```bash
EXECUTIONS_DATA_SAVE_ON_SUCCESS=none        # don't keep phone numbers in execution history
EXECUTIONS_DATA_SAVE_ON_ERROR=all
EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true
EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE=168                 # hours (7 days)
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<from secret manager>    # protects stored credentials
N8N_SECURE_COOKIE=true
```
- Put it behind HTTPS, keep user management on, and turn on MFA for every n8n login.
- Store the WhatsApp token and DB password in n8n Credentials, never in node parameters or Code nodes.
- Host it in an SA region (AWS `af-south-1`, Azure South Africa North/West, GCP `africa-south1`, or a local provider). Then the n8n part isn't a cross-border transfer. **n8n Cloud** is hosted outside SA, so if you use it, record it as an operator (s21 written agreement / DPA) and a **s72** transfer.
- **Meta (WhatsApp Cloud API)** processes messages outside SA either way. Record it in your ROPA as an operator and cross-border transfer, with the s72 ground you rely on (normally its data processing terms, under s72(1)(a)).

ROPA row to add:
```csv
store,fields,data_subjects,purpose,lawful_basis,retention,operators,cross_border,owner
WhatsApp Friday promo,"first_name, phone_e164",customers,Weekly promotions for own products,"s69(1) consent / s69(3) existing customer",send log 12m; consent proof life+3y,"n8n (self-hosted SA), Meta WhatsApp Cloud API",USA/EU (Meta),Marketing lead
```

---

## 5. Message content (s69(4)) and fixing collection going forward

**Meta marketing template `friday_promo_v3`:**
> Hi {{1}}, this Friday's specials at [Trading name]: [offer]. Shop: [link]
>
> From [Registered name (Pty) Ltd] t/a [Trading name], [phone], privacy@yourdomain.co.za. Reply **STOP** to stop promotional messages.
>
> *Button (quick reply):* `Stop promotions`

Every send has to identify you and give contact details for opting out (s69(4)). For existing-customer sends, the in-message opt-out is also a condition of the exception.

**At checkout** (this record makes route 2 work; log it as `optout_offered`):
> ☐ *Don't* send me WhatsApp offers from [Trading name] about [product category]. You can opt out any time by replying STOP.

**For everyone else** (opt-in, Form 4-style; log as `granted` on `marketing_whatsapp` and `whatsapp_platform_optin`):
> ☐ Yes, [Registered name (Pty) Ltd] t/a [Trading name] may send me offers on [product category] by **WhatsApp**. I can withdraw at any time by replying STOP or emailing privacy@yourdomain.co.za.

Leave it unticked, keep it separate from your T&Cs, and link the privacy notice next to it. You may ask a non-customer for consent **once**. If they ignore or refuse it, don't ask again (s69(2)).

---

## What I did by default
- Restricted the audience to s69-eligible customers, checked **at send time**.
- Excluded opted-out numbers across channels, and minors.
- Added a STOP handler and in-message opt-out.
- Gave n8n a least-privilege DB role that can read only the audience view.
- Kept phone numbers out of logs and execution history.
- Added purpose and retention tags, and flagged n8n and Meta for the ROPA and s72.

## I need from you
1. Are all records in `customers` people who actually **bought** something, or does the table include leads or sign-ups?
2. Do you have any record that customers were offered a marketing opt-out when they gave their number? If not, plan a one-time consent request instead of a broadcast.
3. Is every promo about **your own** products similar to what they bought? Partner or third-party offers need opt-in consent.
4. Self-hosted n8n or n8n Cloud?

This is engineering and compliance guidance, not legal advice. If the database holds bought or imported numbers, have a POPIA attorney look at it before you send anything.

must.item: Limits sends to people who opted in or who qualify under the s69(3) customer exception for own similar products
must.reason: States the audience 'can't be' every number, defines s69(1)(a) opt-in and the s69(3) conditions (sale context, own similar products, opt-out offered at collection and in every message, not opted out), and enforces both routes in the whatsapp_promo_audience view.

must.item: Checks consent or opt-out status at send time
must.reason: The audience query 'runs at send time, not when a list was built, so someone who replied STOP on Thursday is excluded on Friday', with withdrawn consent and suppression-table checks in the view.

must.item: Includes sender identity and a working opt-out such as Reply STOP (s69(4))
must.reason: Template includes '[Registered name (Pty) Ltd] t/a [Trading name], [phone]... Reply STOP', a quick-reply button, and a Workflow B STOP handler, citing s69(4) correctly.

must.item: Notes Meta and n8n cloud as operators and cross-border transfers
must.reason: Section 4 says n8n Cloud is hosted outside SA and must be recorded as an operator (s21) and s72 transfer, and Meta WhatsApp Cloud API must be recorded as an operator and cross-border transfer under s72(1)(a).

must_not.item: Sends to all numbers without a consent or customer-exception check
must_not.reason: n8n can only read the eligibility view; leads, bought lists and STOP numbers are excluded.
Explicitly says 'A WhatsApp promo is direct marketing by electronic communication, so s69 applies.'

results.title: Criminal and credit checks on all applicants
results.answer:
Yes, there are significant issues. **Running both checks on every applicant, interns included, is the problem.** Criminal records are special personal information under POPIA, and the National Credit Act limits credit checks to specific kinds of role. You can still run checks, but only role by role, with notice, consent and a vetted vendor.

## 1. Criminal checks: special personal information

**s26** prohibits processing information about a person's **criminal behaviour** (alleged offences or proceedings) unless an authorisation applies. There are two routes.

**s27(1) general authorisations.** You need one of these:
- (a) **consent** of the data subject;
- (b) necessary to establish, exercise or defend a right or obligation in law;
- (c) necessary to comply with an obligation of international public law;
- (d) historical, statistical or research purposes, with public interest and appropriate guarantees;
- (e) information **deliberately made public** by the data subject;
- (f) one of the **specific authorisations** in s28 to s33.

**s33 (criminal behaviour and biometrics), the specific authorisation that matters here.** It allows processing by bodies charged by law with applying criminal law, or by responsible parties that obtained the information in accordance with the law. Processing about personnel must follow the rules set under labour legislation.

**What fits for you:** rely on **s33** *and* get the applicant's **explicit, informed consent (s27(1)(a))** for each check. Grounds (b) to (e) don't realistically apply to routine recruitment screening. Consent only holds up if the check is **justified for the role**:
- **EEA s6(2)(b):** distinguishing on an *inherent requirement of the job* isn't unfair discrimination. A blanket check across every role is hard to defend that way. Childcare, security, healthcare and cash or finance roles usually can be justified. A marketing intern usually can't.
- **s10 minimality:** information that's excessive for the purpose is unlawful even with consent.
- **"Consent" in a job application is fragile.** An applicant who refuses loses the job, so it's questionable whether consent is truly voluntary (s1). That's why the role justification has to stand on its own.

**Two more things to check:**
- **Vendor prior authorisation (s57(1)(b)).** A screening company processing criminal information *on behalf of third parties* (you) needs the Regulator's prior authorisation. Ask for proof before you sign. If your company ever shares adverse findings with other employers (a "blacklist"), you may need it too.
- **Fingerprints are biometrics.** Many SA criminal checks run on fingerprints. That's a second category of special PI (s26). It needs the same s27 and s33 analysis, and the vendor should not keep the prints or templates after the check.

## 2. Credit checks: limited by the National Credit Act

Credit records aren't special PI under POPIA, but the **National Credit Regulations (Reg 18(4)(c) and Reg 19(12); NCR Circular 01 of 2019)** let employers use consumer credit records **only for positions requiring honesty in dealing with cash or finances**, with the job description on file. A credit check on every applicant, or on interns not handling money, falls outside that. It also fails **s10** (excessive) and probably **s11**, because you'd have no valid lawful basis.

For the roles where a credit check is allowed, use **s11(1)(a) consent**. The data comes from a bureau rather than from the applicant, which **s12** allows when they consent to that source.

## 3. Interns: one extra flag

If any interns, job-shadow learners or holiday workers are **under 18**, they're children under **s34**. Processing their information needs a **s35(1)** ground, normally **prior consent of a competent person** (parent or guardian). Running a criminal check on a minor is special PI about a child. **Talk to an attorney before doing it.** In practice, there's almost never a role-based reason to check a school-age intern.

## 4. What compliant screening looks like

| Requirement | Section | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Check matrix by role | s10, EEA s6(2)(b), NCA Reg 19(12) | General staff and interns: ID and qualifications only. Finance or cash roles: add credit, and criminal if an inherent requirement. Childcare, healthcare, security: criminal if an inherent requirement or required by law |
| Tell applicants up front | s18 | Put it in the job ad or application notice: which checks may be run for this role, why, which vendor, how long results are kept, their rights |
| Separate consent per check | s27(1)(a), s11(1)(a) | Unticked and specific ("criminal record check via [vendor]"), recorded with date and wording. Only at shortlist stage, not on the first application form |
| No criminal fields on the application form | s10, s26 | Remove "Do you have a criminal record?" tick boxes from the initial form |
| Vendor due diligence | s21, s57(1)(b), s72 | Written operator agreement, proof of prior authorisation, hosting country (s72 basis if offshore), deletion of fingerprints and extracts |
| Store the result, not the record | s10, s14 | Keep `clear` / `adverse` / `pending` plus the vendor reference. Restrict and delete any full extract quickly |
| Human decision and a chance to respond | s71, fairness | No automatic rejection on an adverse flag. Let the applicant explain or dispute the record (records are sometimes wrong or expunged) |
| Retention | s14 | Results kept until the hiring decision plus a proof period. Unsuccessful applicants' data purged on a schedule (e.g. 6–12 months after the role closes) |
| Access control | s19 | HR only, not line managers. Encrypted at rest. Access logged |

## Bottom line

- **Criminal checks:** permitted only for roles where it's an inherent requirement, with notice, explicit consent, s33 compliance and a vendor with s57(1)(b) authorisation.
- **Credit checks:** only for cash or finance roles.
- **Interns:** neither check by default, and if they're under 18, parental consent is needed as well, with legal advice before any criminal check.

This is engineering and compliance guidance, not legal advice. Screening for special personal information across your whole applicant pool is high-stakes, so have a POPIA or labour attorney sign off your check matrix and consent wording before you roll it out. If it helps, I can draft the role-based check matrix, the applicant notice and the consent wording.

must.item: Notes criminal behaviour information is special personal information (s26, s33)
must.reason: States criminal records are special PI under s26, correctly lists the s27(1) grounds, and describes s33 including the labour-legislation rule for personnel.

must.item: Explains credit checks for employment are limited to positions requiring honesty with cash or finances (NCA regulations)
must.reason: Cites the National Credit Regulations (Reg 19(12), NCR Circular 01 of 2019): use 'only for positions requiring honesty in dealing with cash or finances', and says checking every applicant or interns falls outside that.

must.item: Recommends role-based justification, informing applicants and obtaining consent
must.reason: Gives a role-based check matrix (EEA s6(2)(b) inherent requirement), s18 notice up front, and separate unticked consent per check under s27(1)(a)/s11(1)(a).

must.item: Mentions s57(1)(b) prior authorisation for vendors processing criminal information on behalf of third parties
must.reason: 'A screening company processing criminal information on behalf of third parties (you) needs the Regulator's prior authorisation [s57(1)(b)]. Ask for proof before you sign.'

must_not.item: Says blanket checks for all roles are fine
must_not.reason: Opens by saying running both checks on every applicant 'is the problem' and that a blanket check is hard to defend.

results.title: How big are POPIA fines
results.answer:
**Short answer:** the maximum administrative fine is **R10 million** (s109). A small startup being fined out of the blue is unlikely under how the Regulator currently enforces, because every fine so far has come after an **ignored enforcement notice**. A fine isn't your only exposure, though, and the steps that lead to one are cheap to avoid.

## 1. What POPIA can impose

POPIA has three separate kinds of consequence.

**a) Administrative fine (s109)**
- The Regulator issues an infringement notice for up to **R10 million**.
- Since the 2025 amendments, it can be paid in instalments (Reg 13).

**b) Criminal offences (s100 to s106, penalties in s107)**
- **Up to 10 years' imprisonment, a fine, or both** for the more serious offences:
  - obstructing the Regulator (s100);
  - **failing to comply with an enforcement notice (s103(1))**;
  - s104(2);
  - unlawful acts involving **account numbers** (s105(1));
  - offences by third parties involving account numbers (s106(1), (3), (4)).
- **Up to 12 months' imprisonment, a fine, or both** for the others:
  - failing to notify processing that needs prior authorisation (s59);
  - breaching confidentiality (s101);
  - obstruction-type offences (s102);
  - knowingly or recklessly making a false statement in response to an information notice (s103(2));
  - s104(1).
- These are prosecuted like any other crime. Directors and staff can be personally exposed.

**c) Civil damages (s99)**
- A data subject, or the Regulator on their behalf, can sue for damages **whether or not there was intent or negligence**.
- No statutory cap. Damages can include patrimonial and non-patrimonial loss, aggravated damages, interest and costs.
- The defences are narrow: vis major, consent, the plaintiff's own fault, compliance not reasonably practicable, or a Regulator exemption.
- For a startup with a large user base, a class of claimants after a breach is the scenario that could cost more than R10 million.

## 2. How enforcement actually works (as of October 2026)

The usual sequence is:

> complaint (s74, Form 5) **or** the Regulator's own investigation (s76(3)) **or** an assessment (s89) → investigation → **enforcement notice (s95)** telling you to fix specific things by a deadline → fine and/or prosecution **only if you ignore it**

The Regulator said in August 2026 that if you comply within the notice period, no fine follows under the current framework. It called this a weakness and may seek a change, so don't assume it will stay this way.

**Fines reported so far:**

| Who | Amount | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Department of Justice (DOJCD) | R5m | Ransomware; lapsed security licences (disputed in court) |
| Department of Basic Education | R5m | Publishing matric results (in court, SCA application) |
| Blouberg Local Municipality | R500k, reduced by court to R250k | |
| IEC | R100k | |
| Lancet Laboratories | R100k | Unreported security compromises |
| **FT Rams Consulting** | **R100k** | **Direct marketing: ignoring opt-outs** (being processed) |

Most of these are public bodies. FT Rams is the one to note, because it shows a small private business can be fined. The cause was ordinary marketing behaviour that a user complained about.

## 3. How likely is it for a small startup?

**Being fined:** low, *if* you respond properly when the Regulator writes to you. Every fine so far required an ignored enforcement notice first.

**Ending up on the Regulator's radar:** more likely than founders assume. The common triggers are:
- **A user complaint.** Anyone can lodge one free of charge on Form 5, including public-interest complainants, and they can ask to stay anonymous. Spam marketing, an ignored access or deletion request, or a privacy notice that doesn't match what you do will all do it.
- **A security compromise.** You *must* report it through the eServices portal (s22). The Regulator has received over 8 000 notifications since commencement, with 1 220+ between April and August 2026 alone. A report can lead to an assessment, as happened to SABS after ransomware in 2026.
- **Sector assessments.** Since 2026 the Regulator has written to organisations in selected sectors asking them to *demonstrate* compliance, without any complaint.

**Costs that arrive before any fine:**
- An enforcement notice still means mandatory remediation work on a deadline, often with 90 days to fix things.
- Civil claims under s99 need no fault.
- Enterprise and government clients increasingly ask for POPIA evidence in procurement, so you can lose deals.
- Reputational damage, especially if the Regulator publicises the matter.

## 4. The cheap steps that matter most

These are the things assessments and enforcement notices keep picking up:
1. **Register your Information Officer** on the eServices portal (s55(2)). This is the first thing an assessment checks. The Central Johannesburg TVET College notice in May 2026 included non-registration.
2. **Put a privacy notice at collection** (s18) that matches what your product actually does.
3. **Use opt-in consent for electronic marketing** (s69), with a working unsubscribe that you honour.
4. **Have an incident response plan** and report compromises promptly (s22). Lancet was fined for not reporting.
5. **Handle access, correction and deletion requests** (s23, s24) within a reasonable time.
6. **If an enforcement notice ever arrives, comply within the deadline**, or appeal to the High Court within 30 days (s97). Ignoring it is what turns a fixable problem into a fine or a criminal offence (s103(1)).

This is compliance guidance, not legal advice. If you've already received a letter or notice from the Regulator, get a POPIA attorney involved straight away. I can also run a quick audit of your product against the items above if that helps.

results.title: Hosting on a US cloud
results.answer:
**Yes, you can.** POPIA doesn't require data to stay in South Africa. But storing your customers' data on AWS in us-east-1 (N. Virginia) is a **cross-border transfer under s72**, and AWS is your **operator** under s20 and s21. You need a documented legal basis, the right contract terms, a line in your privacy notice and proper security. If any of the data is **special personal information or children's information**, there's an extra hurdle.

## 1. Pick a s72 ground

You may only transfer personal information to a third party in a foreign country if at least one of these applies (s72(1)):

| Ground | What it means |
|---|---|
| **(a) Adequate protection** | The recipient is bound by a **law, binding corporate rules or a binding agreement** that gives an adequate level of protection, upholding principles substantially similar to POPIA's conditions, including rules on onward transfers |
| **(b) Consent** | The data subject consents to the transfer |
| **(c) Contract with the data subject** | The transfer is necessary to perform a contract between you and the data subject, or for pre-contract steps they asked for |
| **(d) Contract in their interest** | Necessary for a contract between you and a third party that's in the data subject's interest |
| **(e) Their benefit** | The transfer benefits the data subject, it isn't reasonably practicable to get their consent, and they'd likely give it |

**What fits: (a), via a binding agreement.** That's the normal ground for cloud hosting.
- **The US isn't automatically "adequate".** As at October 2026 the Regulator has **not published an adequacy list**, so you can't rely on US law alone. Your protection comes from the contract.
- **Use AWS's data processing terms (DPA)** as the binding agreement. Read them against POPIA and check:
  - security obligations;
  - prompt breach notification to you;
  - restrictions on sub-processors and onward transfers;
  - deletion when you leave.
- **Watch for juristic persons.** EU-style clauses (GDPR SCCs) help, but they only cover natural persons. POPIA also protects **juristic persons**, such as your business customers' company data. If AWS's terms don't extend to them, note the gap and how you're covering it.
- **Write down your assessment.** A short internal note on why you consider the protection adequate is enough. Include practical factors such as encryption with keys you control. The burden is on you to show the ground applies.

**Why the others are weak here:**
- **(b) Consent** can be withdrawn, and if a customer does, you can't easily move only their data out of us-east-1.
- **(c)** means "necessary", not "convenient". A US region is almost never *necessary* to give a South African customer your service when SA regions exist.
- **(d) and (e)** don't fit routine hosting.

## 2. Everything else you need

| Requirement | Section | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Operator contract | s21(1) | Written terms obliging AWS to maintain s19 security measures. The AWS Customer Agreement plus DPA usually covers this; keep a copy on file |
| Breach notification from the operator | s21(2) | Confirm AWS will notify you of unauthorised access. You stay responsible for notifying the Regulator (eServices portal) and your customers (s22) |
| Tell customers | s18(1)(g) | In your privacy notice: "Your information is stored with Amazon Web Services in the United States, under contractual safeguards substantially similar to POPIA" |
| Security on your side | s19 | Encryption at rest (KMS) and TLS in transit, least-privilege IAM, MFA on the root and all IAM users, no public S3 buckets, CloudTrail on, backups encrypted with a defined retention. AWS secures the cloud itself; configuration is your responsibility |
| Record it | s17 | Add a ROPA / operator register row: AWS, us-east-1, which data stores, DPA in place, s72(1)(a), date reviewed |
| Onward transfers | s72(1)(a) | Know which AWS services you use. Some features (e.g. global services, CloudFront edge logs, AI services) may process data in other regions |

## 3. The extra hurdle: special personal information and children's information

If you store **special personal information** (health, biometrics, religion, race, criminal records, union membership, political views, sex life) or **children's information** (under 18), and the destination lacks adequate protection, you need the Regulator's **prior authorisation under s57(1)(d)** *before* transferring it. It's applied for online, and processing must wait for the Regulator's decision (4 weeks, extendable up to 13).

Since there's no adequacy finding for the US, **talk to a POPIA attorney before putting this kind of data in us-east-1.** The simpler option is to keep it in an SA region.

## 4. Consider just using Cape Town

AWS has an SA region, **`af-south-1` (Cape Town)**. Hosting there means:
- **no s72 analysis** for that data store (AWS is still an operator, so the s21 contract still applies);
- no s57(1)(d) question for special or children's data;
- a simpler privacy notice and easier enterprise and government procurement.

Prices are higher and not every AWS service is available there, so check the services you need. A common setup is customer personal information in `af-south-1`, with non-personal workloads (static assets, build pipelines) wherever is cheapest.

If you're a **regulated financial institution**, also check sector rules on offshoring and cloud (e.g. the FSCA/PA joint standards) before choosing a region.

## Checklist
- [ ] Rely on s72(1)(a): read AWS's DPA, record the adequacy assessment, and note the juristic-person gap if there is one
- [ ] Have s21 operator terms on file
- [ ] Disclose the US transfer in your privacy notice (s18(1)(g))
- [ ] Apply s19 security baseline (KMS, IAM least privilege, MFA, private buckets, CloudTrail)
- [ ] Add a ROPA / operator register entry with region and s72 ground
- [ ] Don't send special or children's personal information to us-east-1 without s57(1)(d) authorisation or legal advice; otherwise use `af-south-1`

This is compliance guidance, not legal advice. If I know which data you'll store and which AWS services you use, I can draft the privacy-notice wording and the operator register entry.
